# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 7, 2026
**Re:** Topar Medical Systems, Inc. / sale of Celestra Imaging Systems, Inc. to Pritor Healthcare Partners, LLC: seller-side exposure review and recommended changes

**Privileged & Confidential: Attorney Work Product**

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed four documents:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated March 16, 2026 (the **SPA**);
- the Bill of Sale and Assignment and Assumption Agreement between Topar and Celestra, effective March 30, 2026 (the **Bill of Sale**);
- the draft Escrow Agreement with Ashcombe Trust Company, N.A. (the **Escrow Agreement**); and
- the Norrland liquid helium supply agreement.

The main deal terms are:

- a Purchase Price of **$186,000,000**;
- a Closing payment of $155,400,000;
- an **$18,600,000** Escrow Amount, held for 18 months; and
- a **$12,000,000** Deferred Payment, due 12 months after Closing.

Three issues need to be fixed before Topar signs anything further. In order of priority:

1. **Uncapped, open-ended product liability indemnity, including for systems Buyer sells after Closing** (SPA §§ 9.2(c), 9.5(c), and the "Specified Matters" definition). Topar's exposure has no ceiling and no time limit. It also extends to a business Topar will no longer own or control.

2. **The Escrow Agreement silently caps Buyer's payment and escrow-release obligations at $5,000,000** (Escrow Agreement § 8.3, operating through SPA § 11.9).
   - Under the SPA, Buyer's obligations to pay the $12,000,000 Deferred Payment and to release the $18,600,000 escrow sit outside the $5,000,000 Buyer Cap.
   - The Escrow Agreement brings them back under that cap.
   - The SPA's precedence clause lets the Escrow Agreement win.
   - As a result, up to $30,600,000 of consideration owed to Topar may be recoverable only up to $5,000,000.

3. **The Okavi reconstruction software license requires Okavi's consent to both the Bill of Sale assignment and the change of control. No consent has been obtained or scheduled** (Bill of Sale § 2.1 and Annex A, Item 1; SPA § 4.4 and Disclosure Schedule 4.4).
   - Topar's "no consents" representation is inaccurate.
   - The assignment may be void.
   - Okavi may terminate a license that is core to Celestra's CT/MRI products.

The Norrland helium supply agreement raises no issue for Topar (see Part III). Open questions for the client and for Pritor are collected in Part IV.

---

## II. Issues

### Issue 1: Uncapped Specified Matters indemnity reaches post-Closing product liability

**Where it appears.** SPA, Article I (definition of "Specified Matters"), Section 9.2(c) and Section 9.5(c). Sections 9.1 and 9.6 are also relevant.

**What the documents say.**

- Section 9.2(c) requires Seller to indemnify Buyer, the Company and their Affiliates for all Losses arising out of "any Specified Matters."
- "Specified Matters" means:
  - (a) any Product Liability Claim relating to any CT or MRI system or component "manufactured, sold or serviced by the Company, **whether before or after the Closing Date**"; and
  - (b) any related recall, field safety corrective action or market withdrawal.
- Section 9.5(c) provides that the Seller Cap in Section 9.5(a) (**$18,600,000**) and the $1,860,000 deductible in Section 9.5(b) "**shall not apply to Losses under Section 9.2(c)**."

**Why it matters to Topar.**

- **No dollar ceiling.** Section 9.5(a) caps Seller's liability only under Section 9.2(a). Its Purchase Price ceiling is framed around Fundamental Representations, and Section 9.5(c) expressly takes Section 9.2(c) out of the Section 9.5(a) cap. At best, Topar has an argument that the Purchase Price is an outer limit. It should not rely on that argument.
- **The risk is Buyer's, not Topar's.** Read together, these provisions make Topar the product liability insurer of Celestra's entire future output and service business. That covers:
  - every CT/MRI system Pritor causes Celestra to design, build, sell or service after Closing;
  - systems built to designs Pritor changes;
  - systems built in facilities Topar no longer runs; and
  - systems built under quality systems Topar no longer controls.

  Topar loses all ability to manage that risk at Closing.
- **Not limited to the escrow.** Section 9.6 says Seller claims are satisfied first from Escrow Funds and then "directly by Seller." The $18,600,000 escrow is therefore a first source of recovery, not a limit.
- **No time limit.** Section 9.1 limits survival of representations (18 months) and covenants (until performed). It says nothing about Section 9.2(c). The Specified Matters indemnity therefore appears to run indefinitely, for the life of every installed system.
- **Recalls are included.** Limb (b) includes field corrections and market withdrawals "undertaken by the Company." That lets Buyer decide on a post-Closing recall and pass the cost to Topar.
- **Overlap with the representations.** Known pre-Closing claims and recalls are already disclosed under Section 4.8 and Schedule 4.8. A capped Section 9.2(a) claim would already cover any inaccuracy there. Section 9.2(c) turns that into uncapped exposure.

**Recommended fix.** Our principal position should cover four points:

1. **Limit Specified Matters to pre-Closing products.** Coverage should reach only systems the Company sold, or service it performed, before Closing.
2. **Bring Specified Matters under a cap.** The cap should be the $18,600,000 Seller Cap, or a lower dedicated sub-cap. Section 9.5(c) should be confined to fraud.
3. **Add a survival period.** For example, a fixed period running from the Closing Date.
4. **Add a reverse indemnity.** Buyer should indemnify Topar for product liability on post-Closing products. Plaintiffs may name Topar as the former parent, so this protection matters.

Proposed language:

> **"Specified Matters"** means (a) any Product Liability Claim relating to any CT or MRI imaging system, or any component of one, that was sold and shipped by the Company, or any servicing performed by the Company, in each case **prior to the Closing Date**, and (b) any recall, field safety corrective action or market withdrawal of any such system **required by a Governmental Authority** in connection with such a Product Liability Claim. For the avoidance of doubt, Specified Matters exclude any Product Liability Claim, recall, field safety corrective action or market withdrawal relating to any system or component manufactured, sold or shipped, or any servicing performed, on or after the Closing Date, whether or not of a design existing before the Closing Date.

> **9.5(c)** *Exceptions to Seller Limitations.* The deductible in Section 9.5(b) shall not apply to Losses under Section 9.2(c). The cap in Section 9.5(a) shall apply to the aggregate of Losses under Sections 9.2(a) and 9.2(c), except that such cap shall not apply to Losses arising from fraud by Seller.

> **9.1** … Claims under Section 9.2(c) may be made only if written notice is given before the date that is [__] months after the Closing Date.

> **9.3(c)** [Buyer shall indemnify Seller and its Affiliates against all Losses arising out of] any Product Liability Claim, recall, field safety corrective action or market withdrawal relating to any system or component manufactured, sold or shipped, or any servicing performed, by the Company on or after the Closing Date.

The Section 9.3(c) reverse indemnity would need to be carved out of the Buyer Cap.

**Fallback positions:**

- Accept a dedicated Specified Matters sub-cap above the general cap, but still within a fixed survival period.
- Cover post-Closing sales of legacy designs only for an initial window, and only for design defects that existed at Closing. Defects introduced by Buyer would be excluded.
- In all cases, Losses would be calculated net of the Company's product liability insurance. Section 9.5(g) already provides for this.

---

### Issue 2: Escrow Agreement § 8.3 strips the Buyer Cap carve-outs and controls through SPA § 11.9

**Where it appears.** The primary provision is Escrow Agreement Section 8.3. It operates together with SPA Sections 9.5(d), 9.5(e) and 11.9.

**What the documents say.**

- **SPA Section 9.5(d)** caps Buyer's aggregate liability under Section 9.3 at **$5,000,000** (the Buyer Cap). Section 9.3(b) expressly covers Buyer's obligations under Sections 2.3 (escrow) and 2.4 (Deferred Payment).
- **SPA Section 9.5(e)** carves three things out of the Buyer Cap:
  - (i) fraud;
  - (ii) Buyer's obligation to pay the Purchase Price, including the **$12,000,000 Deferred Payment**; and
  - (iii) Buyer's obligation to deliver joint written instructions releasing Escrow Funds.
- **Escrow Agreement Section 8.3** provides that Buyer's aggregate liability to Seller "arising under or in connection with this Escrow Agreement or Article IX of the Purchase Agreement, **including with respect to release of Escrow Funds, shall not exceed the Buyer Cap, except for fraud**." It keeps only the fraud carve-out. It drops carve-outs (ii) and (iii).
- **SPA Section 11.9** provides that, where the SPA and the Escrow Agreement conflict, "the Escrow Agreement shall prevail with respect to releases of Escrow Funds and the limitations of liability stated therein."

**Why it matters to Topar.**

- **The Escrow Agreement wins the conflict.** Section 8.3 is a "limitation of liability stated therein," and it expressly addresses releases of Escrow Funds. Under Section 11.9 it therefore controls over SPA Section 9.5(e). We should not assume the SPA carve-outs survive. On the documents as drafted, the better reading is that they do not.
- **Escrow release exposure.**
  - Release of the escrow depends entirely on Buyer co-signing Joint Written Instructions (Escrow Agreement §§ 3.2–3.4, 4.2 and 4.3).
  - The Escrow Agent will not act without those instructions or a Final Order (§§ 3.3 and 6.4).
  - If Buyer refuses to sign, or files inflated Claim Notices to tie up the $18,600,000, Topar's damages for that breach would be capped at $5,000,000.
  - Under Section 4.2, the Pending Claim Amount is held back automatically, so a Buyer acting in bad faith has real leverage.
- **Deferred Payment exposure.**
  - The $12,000,000 Deferred Payment is a Buyer covenant that Section 9.3(b) indemnifies.
  - Section 8.3 reaches liability "in connection with … Article IX of the Purchase Agreement."
  - Buyer will argue that its liability for non-payment is therefore capped at $5,000,000.
- **Topar's counterarguments are not reliable.** Topar can argue that:
  - a claim for the Deferred Payment is a direct contract claim for the price, not an Article IX claim (SPA § 9.8 preserves "claims for payment of the Deferred Payment" outside the exclusive remedy); and
  - specific performance under SPA § 11.8 is not "liability."

  These are litigation positions, and Section 8.3's breadth ("arising under or in connection with") cuts against them.
- **Combined effect.** Roughly **$30,600,000** of Topar's consideration ($18,600,000 escrow plus $12,000,000 Deferred Payment) could be enforceable as damages only up to $5,000,000.
- **It can still be fixed.** The Escrow Agreement is undated and unsigned. It is a Seller closing deliverable under SPA § 3.2(b), so the drafting can be corrected now.

**Recommended fix.** We should do both of the following. Either alone would help, but together they leave no conflict for Section 11.9 to resolve against Topar.

**(a) Conform Escrow Agreement Section 8.3 to SPA Section 9.5(e):**

> **8.3 Liability of Buyer.** The limitations on the liability of Buyer to Seller under this Escrow Agreement and Article IX of the Purchase Agreement shall be as set out in Sections 9.5(d) and 9.5(e) of the Purchase Agreement. Without limiting the foregoing, the Buyer Cap shall not apply to (i) Losses arising from fraud by Buyer, (ii) Buyer's obligation to pay the Purchase Price, including the Deferred Payment, or (iii) Buyer's obligations to deliver Joint Written Instructions for the release of Escrow Funds under this Escrow Agreement or the Purchase Agreement.

Alternatively, delete Section 8.3 entirely, since the Escrow Agent does not need it.

**(b) Narrow SPA Section 11.9** so the Escrow Agreement controls only on the Escrow Agent's mechanics:

> **11.9 Order of Precedence.** In the event of any conflict between this Agreement and the Bill of Sale, this Agreement shall prevail. In the event of any conflict between this Agreement and the Escrow Agreement, (a) the Escrow Agreement shall prevail solely with respect to the rights, duties, protections and procedures of the Escrow Agent in holding, investing and disbursing the Escrow Funds, and (b) this Agreement shall prevail in all other respects, including with respect to the rights and obligations of Buyer and Seller as between themselves and any limitation on the liability of either of them.

**Further protection.** Consider adding an express covenant that Buyer will not deliver a Claim Notice except in good faith. Buyer should also bear Topar's costs, and interest at the Section 2.4 rate, on any escrow amount that is wrongfully withheld.

---

### Issue 3: Okavi license requires consent to the assignment and the change of control, and none has been obtained or scheduled

**Where it appears.** The primary provisions are Bill of Sale Section 2.1 and Annex A, Item 1, which quotes Okavi license Section 14.2. The issue also affects:

- SPA Section 4.4 and Disclosure Schedule 4.4;
- SPA Sections 3.2, 4.6, 6.2, 7.2(a) and 9.2(a); and
- Bill of Sale Section 6(b).

**What the documents say.**

- Bill of Sale Section 2.1 assigns all Contract Rights to Celestra, effective March 30, 2026. That expressly includes the Reconstruction Software License Agreement with Okavi Algorithms GmbH. This license covers the low-dose CT and accelerated MRI iterative reconstruction modules embedded in Celestra's systems, with term through May 31, 2029.
- License Section 14.2, quoted in Annex A, has three parts:
  - Licensee may not assign or transfer the license "without the **prior written consent of Licensor**";
  - "**any change of control of Licensee**, including any transfer of more than fifty percent (50%) of the voting securities of Licensee," is deemed a transfer requiring consent; and
  - any non-compliant transfer "shall be null and void, and Licensor may terminate this Agreement immediately upon written notice."
- **SPA Section 4.4** represents that neither the SPA nor the Bill of Sale requires any consent under any contract, "including the Assigned Contracts," or gives rise to a termination right, "except as set out in Schedule 4.4." **Disclosure Schedule 4.4 reads "None."**
- The Seller closing deliverables in **SPA Section 3.2** include no Okavi consent.

**Why it matters to Topar.** The transaction trips the consent requirement twice:

- **Assignment.** The Bill of Sale transfers the license from Topar to Celestra.
- **Change of control.** Once Celestra is the licensee, the sale of 100% of its stock to Pritor is a change of control of the Licensee.

The consequences for Topar are:

- **Inaccurate representation and bring-down risk.**
  - Section 4.4 is untrue as of signing and, unless cured, as of Closing.
  - Section 4.4 is not a Fundamental Representation, but a failure to obtain consent for core reconstruction software is very likely material.
  - Buyer would then have a walk right under Section 7.2(a) and a termination right under Section 8.1(c).
- **Post-Closing indemnity claim.**
  - The breach can be indemnified under Section 9.2(a), subject to the $1,860,000 deductible and the $18,600,000 cap, recoverable first from the escrow.
  - The SPA has no anti-sandbagging clause, so Buyer can close knowing of the defect and still claim.
  - Topar also gave a separate representation in Bill of Sale Section 6(b).
- **Loss of the license.**
  - The assignment may already be void if the Bill of Sale has been signed and become effective.
  - Okavi can terminate immediately.
  - Celestra embeds and ships Okavi software, paying a per-unit royalty. A void assignment could leave Celestra shipping systems without a license, which risks infringement claims and supply disruption.
  - Those consequences flow back to Topar as indemnifiable Losses. They also make Okavi's leverage in any consent negotiation significant.
- **Schedule 4.6 does not cure the problem.** It lists the Assigned Contracts as material contracts, but it is not a disclosure of the consent requirement under Section 4.4.

**Recommended fix.**

1. **Approach Okavi now** for a written consent. The consent should, in one instrument:
   - consent to the assignment to Celestra under the Bill of Sale, with effect from March 30, 2026;
   - consent to the change of control of Celestra resulting from the SPA;
   - waive any termination right arising from either event; and
   - confirm the license is in full force and effect.
2. **Correct the Disclosure Schedule**:

   > **Schedule 4.4 — Consents.** 1. Consent of Okavi Algorithms GmbH under Section 14.2 of the Reconstruction Software License Agreement dated June 1, 2022 (as amended by Amendment No. 1 dated September 12, 2024) to (a) the assignment of that agreement to the Company under the Bill of Sale and (b) the change of control of the Company resulting from the sale of the Shares under this Agreement.

3. **Add a closing deliverable**, with a matching efforts covenant:

   > **3.2(i)** a copy of the written consent of Okavi Algorithms GmbH described in Item 1 of Schedule 4.4, in form reasonably satisfactory to Buyer.

   > **6.7 Third-Party Consents.** Seller shall use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain, before the Closing, the consents listed on Schedule 4.4; provided that neither Seller nor the Company shall be required to pay any consent fee or agree to any amendment adverse to the Company without Buyer's consent [and, if Buyer withholds such consent, any resulting failure shall not constitute a breach of Section 4.4].

4. **Coordinate timing.** If the Bill of Sale has not yet been signed, do not sign it, or make its Okavi assignment conditional, until consent is in hand. If it has been signed, confirm the scope and timing of the Section 5.1 counterparty notices sent to Okavi.
5. **Request a specific carve-out.** Ask Buyer to agree that any Losses arising from Okavi matters disclosed on the updated Schedule 4.4 are excluded from Section 9.2(a).

---

## III. Documents reviewed with no material issue for Topar

- **Norrland Liquid Helium Supply Agreement (Celestra as Customer).**
  - Section 14.1 expressly provides that a change in ownership or control of either Party "is not an assignment … and does not require the consent of the other Party." The stock sale therefore needs no Norrland consent, and Schedule 4.4 is accurate on this point.
  - The obligations stay with Celestra and pass economically to Buyer through the stock sale. These include the 60,000-liter Minimum Annual Volume and the related shortfall payment (§ 2.2).
  - No action is needed beyond confirming that the agreement appears on Schedule 4.6 if it meets the $500,000 threshold.
- **Other Assigned Contracts (Bill of Sale, Annex A, Items 2 and 3).**
  - The Meridell subscription may be assigned to an Affiliate or successor on notice.
  - The Halvren license may be assigned without consent on notice.
  - Neither contains a change-of-control restriction as summarized. The only step needed is confirming that the Section 5.1 notices were sent.

---

## IV. Open questions (client and/or Pritor input required)

1. **Deal status and outside date.** SPA Section 8.1(b) permits either party to terminate if Closing has not occurred by **July 31, 2026**. That date has passed.
   - *Confirm with client:* has the outside date been extended in writing, and has Closing occurred?
   - Our recommendations assume Closing has not occurred and that the SPA can still be amended. If Closing has occurred, the analysis shifts to post-Closing amendment and dispute posture.
2. **Bill of Sale execution.** *Confirm with client* whether the Bill of Sale was actually signed and became effective on March 30, 2026, and whether the Section 5.1 notice went to Okavi. This determines whether the Okavi assignment may already be void and whether termination risk is already live.
3. **Okavi relationship and license terms.**
   - *Confirm with client* whether Okavi has been contacted or has signaled a position.
   - Ask whether Okavi is likely to seek a consent fee or a royalty increase.
   - We have only the Annex A excerpt. Obtain the full license and Amendment No. 1 to confirm Section 14.2 is unchanged and to check whether affiliate sublicensing is permitted as an interim bridge.
4. **Commercial position on Specified Matters.**
   - *Confirm with client* why Topar agreed to Section 9.2(c) and whether Pritor priced it in. This tells us how hard we can push.
   - Obtain the Schedule 4.8 claims and recall history and Celestra's product liability and recall insurance, including tail or run-off options.
   - Ask whether Topar would accept a sub-cap or time-limited coverage for legacy designs as a fallback.
5. **Escrow Agreement drafting history.** *Ask Pritor's counsel* whether Section 8.3 was intended to depart from SPA Section 9.5(e). If they say it was not, a conforming change should be uncontroversial. If they say it was, that is a re-trade of agreed economics and should be escalated.
6. **Status of Buyer's financing for the Deferred Payment.** Section 5.3 contains a sufficiency-of-funds representation. *Confirm with client* whether Topar wants credit support, such as a parent guarantee or letter of credit, for the $12,000,000 Deferred Payment. This matters particularly given the Issue 2 cap risk.

---

## V. Recommended next steps

1. Send Pritor a mark-up covering:
   - the "Specified Matters" definition and SPA §§ 9.1, 9.3 and 9.5(c);
   - Escrow Agreement § 8.3; and
   - SPA § 11.9.
2. In parallel, open the Okavi consent process and update Schedule 4.4, § 3.2 and the related covenant.
3. Resolve Open Questions 1 and 2 with the client immediately, because they determine whether we are negotiating pre-Closing amendments or managing post-Closing exposure.

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Supervising Partner
**From:** [Associate]
**Date:** November 7, 2026
**Re:** Topar Medical Systems, Inc. – Sale of Celestra Imaging Systems, Inc. to Pritor Healthcare Partners, LLC – Seller-Side Exposure Review

---

## I. Summary

I reviewed four documents:

- the Stock Purchase Agreement dated March 16, 2026 (the "**SPA**");
- the Bill of Sale and Assignment and Assumption Agreement from Topar to Celestra, effective March 30, 2026 (the "**Bill of Sale**");
- the draft Escrow Agreement with Ashcombe Trust Company, N.A. (the "**Escrow Agreement**"); and
- the Norrland liquid helium supply agreement (the "**Helium Agreement**").

Two issues need to be fixed before Closing, in priority order:

1. **Uncapped product liability indemnity that reaches post-Closing sales.** This is the highest priority. SPA §§9.2(c) and 9.5(c), read together, make Topar liable without limit for product liability claims. That includes claims on CT/MRI systems that Pritor causes Celestra to build, sell or service after Closing, when Topar has no control over the business.

2. **Okavi license consent has not been obtained or disclosed.** This is also high priority. The Okavi reconstruction software license requires Okavi's prior written consent in two situations:
   - to the assignment made by the Bill of Sale; and
   - to the change of control caused by the stock sale.

   No consent is scheduled or listed as a closing deliverable. As a result, SPA §4.4 and Disclosure Schedule 4.4 ("None") are inaccurate. Topar faces an indemnity claim and Celestra could lose core imaging software.

Several points also need client or counterparty input. These are listed in Part IV. The most important is a **timing question**. The SPA's outside date in §8.1(b) was July 31, 2026, and that date has passed. We need to confirm whether the SPA was extended and where the deal stands.

The Helium Agreement does not raise any concern for this transaction (see Part III.B).

### Key commercial terms (for reference)

| Term | Amount / Provision | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Purchase Price | $186,000,000 | SPA §2.1 |
| Closing Payment | $155,400,000 | SPA §2.2 |
| Deferred Payment | $12,000,000, payable 12 months after Closing | SPA §2.4 |
| Escrow Amount | $18,600,000 | SPA §1.1; Escrow Agt. §2.1 |
| Escrow Period | 18 months after Closing | Escrow Agt. §4.1 |
| Seller indemnity cap (rep breaches) | $18,600,000 | SPA §9.5(a) |
| Deductible | $1,860,000 (non-Fundamental reps) | SPA §9.5(b) |
| Buyer Cap | $5,000,000 | SPA §9.5(d) |
| General rep survival | 18 months after Closing | SPA §9.1 |

---

## II. Priority Issues

### Issue 1 – Uncapped "Specified Matters" indemnity reaches post-Closing product liability

**Where it appears:**
- SPA §1.1, definition of "Specified Matters";
- SPA §9.2(c) (indemnity for Specified Matters); and
- SPA §9.5(c) (exceptions to Seller limitations).

**What the documents say:**
- **§1.1.** "Specified Matters" includes any Product Liability Claim relating to any CT or MRI system or component "manufactured, sold or serviced by the Company, **whether before or after the Closing Date**." It also includes any related recall, field safety corrective action or market withdrawal.
- **§9.2(c).** Seller must indemnify Buyer, the Company and their Affiliates for all Losses arising out of any Specified Matters.
- **§9.5(c).** The $18,600,000 cap in §9.5(a) and the $1,860,000 deductible in §9.5(b) "**shall not apply to Losses under Section 9.2(c)**."

**Why it matters to Topar:**

- **Topar would insure the buyer's own business.** Read together, these provisions turn Topar into an open-ended product liability insurer of Celestra's business after Closing.
  - Every system Pritor causes Celestra to design, manufacture, sell or service after Closing falls inside the indemnity.
  - That holds even if the defect comes from Pritor's own design changes, suppliers, quality system or servicing practices.
  - Topar will have no control over any of those things.

- **There is no limit.** The exposure has no cap, no deductible and no time limit.
  - §9.5(c) disapplies "the cap in Section 9.5(a)" as a whole. Buyer can therefore argue that even the Purchase Price ceiling inside §9.5(a) does not reach §9.2(c) Losses. On that reading the exposure could exceed the $186,000,000 Topar receives.
  - §9.1 limits survival only for representations and warranties. Covenants survive "until fully performed." The §9.2(c) indemnity does not fit cleanly into either category, so Buyer will argue it survives indefinitely.

- **The type of loss is severe.** CT and MRI claims can involve personal injury, radiation dose and magnet or cryogen incidents. "Losses" includes recalls and field corrections, which run across the installed base. These can be very costly.

- **The escrow is no protection.** §9.6 directs recovery first from the Escrow Funds and then directly from Topar "subject to Section 9.5." Because §9.5 does not limit §9.2(c), Topar's exposure goes well beyond the $18,600,000 Escrow Amount.

- **Buyer is already protected for pre-Closing matters.** Product Liability Claims arising from pre-Closing conduct are covered by the §4.8 representation through §9.2(a). The post-Closing reach of §9.2(c) has no legitimate pre-Closing risk-allocation rationale.

**Recommended fix (in order of preference):**

1. **Limit Specified Matters to pre-Closing products and services.** Proposed language:

   > "**Specified Matters**" means (a) any Product Liability Claim relating to any CT or MRI imaging system, or any component of one, to the extent such system or component was manufactured and sold by the Company, or the relevant servicing was performed by the Company, **prior to the Closing Date**, and (b) any recall, field safety corrective action or market withdrawal of any such system required by a Governmental Authority **with respect to a defect existing as of the Closing Date**; *provided* that Specified Matters shall not include any Losses to the extent arising from any modification, servicing, labeling change, software update or other act or omission of Buyer, the Company or their Affiliates after the Closing.

2. **Bring Specified Matters under the cap.** Amend §9.5(c) to remove the reference to §9.2(c), and add §9.2(c) to the cap. Proposed language:

   > (a) *Seller Cap.* The aggregate liability of Seller under Sections 9.2(a) **and 9.2(c)** shall not exceed $18,600,000 …
   >
   > (c) *Exceptions to Seller Limitations.* The deductible in Section 9.5(b) shall not apply to Losses under Section 9.2(c). The cap in Section 9.5(a) shall not apply to Losses arising from fraud by Seller.

   *Fallback:* If Buyer insists on a separate Specified Matters cap, agree to a separate cap, but keep it within an overall Purchase Price ceiling.

3. **Add a time limit.** Specified Matters claims should be brought within a defined period after Closing. For example, use the 18-month general survival period, or a negotiated longer period tied to the products' expected service life.

4. **Add a reciprocal Buyer indemnity.** Add a new §9.3(c) under which Buyer indemnifies Seller for Product Liability Claims relating to systems manufactured, sold or serviced after Closing. This protects Topar where a claimant sues Topar as former parent.

5. **Net out insurance.** Confirm that §9.5(g) (net of insurance) applies, and consider requiring Buyer to maintain products/completed-operations coverage after Closing.

---

### Issue 2 – Okavi license: assignment and change-of-control consent not obtained or scheduled

**Where it appears:**
- Bill of Sale §2.1 and Annex A, Item 1 (Okavi Reconstruction Software License, §14.2);
- SPA §4.4 and Disclosure Schedule 4.4;
- SPA §3.2 (Seller closing deliverables); and
- SPA §§4.6 and 7.2(a).

**What the documents say:**
- **Bill of Sale §2.1.** Assigns to Celestra all Contract Rights, "includ[ing] Assignor's rights under the Reconstruction Software License Agreement with Okavi Algorithms GmbH."
- **Okavi license §14.2 (quoted in Annex A).** Provides that:
  - Licensee may not assign or transfer the license "without the **prior written consent of Licensor**";
  - "**any change of control of Licensee**, including any transfer of more than fifty percent (50%) of the voting securities of Licensee," is a transfer requiring consent; and
  - any non-compliant transfer "shall be null and void," and Okavi "may terminate this Agreement immediately upon written notice."
- **SPA §4.4.** Seller represents that no consent is required under any contract, "including the Assigned Contracts," and no termination right is triggered, except as listed on Schedule 4.4. **Schedule 4.4 reads "None."**
- **SPA §3.2.** The closing deliverables do not include any Okavi consent.

**Why it matters to Topar:**

- **Consent is needed twice.**
  - *First trigger (the Bill of Sale).* Topar's assignment to Celestra, effective March 30, 2026, is a transfer that requires Okavi's consent.
  - *Second trigger (the stock sale).* Once the license sits in Celestra, the sale of 100% of Celestra's stock to Pritor is a change of control of the *Licensee* under §14.2.
  - A consent to the first step will not necessarily cover the second. We need a consent that expressly covers both.

- **The assignment may already be void.** If the Bill of Sale has been signed, the assignment may be void under §14.2. If so:
  - the license may still sit with Topar, or Okavi may be entitled to terminate it;
  - this defeats SPA §6.2; and
  - it makes Topar's Bill of Sale §6(b) representation (each Assigned Contract "is in full force and effect") vulnerable.

- **Okavi may already know.** Bill of Sale §5.1 required joint notice to each counterparty within ten Business Days after March 30, 2026. If that notice went to Okavi, Okavi is on notice of an unconsented transfer.

- **Topar's representations are inaccurate.**
  - §4.4 and Schedule 4.4 are inaccurate as of signing.
  - The §4.6 representation that each listed contract (including each Assigned Contract) is in full force and effect is also at risk.
  - The representations are brought down at Closing.

- **The consequences:**
  - *Closing risk.* The §7.2(a) closing condition may fail, which gives Pritor leverage to reprice or walk away.
  - *Indemnity.* After Closing, Pritor can claim under §9.2(a). §4.4 is not a Fundamental Representation, so the $1,860,000 deductible and $18,600,000 cap apply. Even so, a claim could consume a large part of the escrow. The materiality scrape in §9.5(f) makes the claim easier to bring.
  - *Commercial loss.* The Okavi software supplies Celestra's low-dose CT and accelerated MRI reconstruction modules and is embedded in shipped systems. Losing it could disrupt production and installed-base support. Pritor would claim lost value as Losses.

**Recommended fix:**

1. **Get Okavi's written consent before Closing.** The consent should cover all of the following:
   - the assignment from Topar to Celestra under the Bill of Sale (ideally with ratification effective March 30, 2026);
   - the change of control of Celestra resulting from the sale to Pritor; and
   - a waiver of any termination right arising from either event.

   Proposed consent language:

   > "Okavi Algorithms GmbH hereby (i) consents to the assignment of the Reconstruction Software License Agreement dated June 1, 2022, as amended, by Topar Medical Systems, Inc. to Celestra Imaging Systems, Inc., effective as of March 30, 2026, and ratifies such assignment as of that date; (ii) consents to the sale of all of the outstanding capital stock of Celestra Imaging Systems, Inc. to Pritor Healthcare Partners, LLC, and agrees that such transaction shall not constitute a breach of, or give rise to any right of termination under, Section 14.2 or any other provision of the Agreement; and (iii) confirms that the Agreement is in full force and effect and that no default exists thereunder."

2. **Update Schedule 4.4 now.** Pritor must agree to the change because the representation speaks as of signing. Proposed language:

   > "**Schedule 4.4 — Consents.** 1. Consent of Okavi Algorithms GmbH under Section 14.2 of the Reconstruction Software License Agreement dated June 1, 2022, as amended September 12, 2024, to (a) the assignment of that agreement to the Company under the Bill of Sale and (b) the change of control of the Company resulting from the sale of the Shares."

   Pair this with an express acknowledgment from Buyer that the Schedule 4.4 update cures any breach of §4.4 and §4.6 relating to the Okavi license, both as of signing and at Closing.

3. **Add a closing deliverable.** Insert a new §3.2(i): "the written consent of Okavi Algorithms GmbH described in Schedule 4.4, in form reasonably satisfactory to Buyer." Agreeing a form now avoids a Closing-day dispute.

4. **Fallback if consent cannot be obtained in time:**
   - negotiate a specific, capped special indemnity in place of an open rep-breach claim; or
   - agree an interim arrangement under which Topar holds the license for Celestra's benefit, if Okavi will permit it.

   Either option needs to be paired with a covenant to use commercially reasonable efforts to obtain consent after Closing.
